Been testing Opus 5.5 to rebuild my ENTIRE Faceless AI Avatar production workflow…

And gotta say this is lowkey insane.

So here’s an 8-step prompting protocol I’m using to scale 6-figure channels with it:

(Abusing the fact it’s cheaper, faster, and better than Fable 5.1…)

Prompt 1: the channel brain (run once per channel)

Create a Claude Project. Upload your 10 best competitor transcripts, your analytics export, your top 20 outlier titles and your thumbnail references. Then:

"Act as the head of production for this faceless YouTube channel. Read everything uploaded and build a channel bible covering: target viewer (age, country, device, when they watch), the emotional promise of every video, recurring story structures, title formulas, thumbnail rules, narrator tone, pacing rules and banned phrases. Include: no em dashes, no rhetorical questions as transitions, no 'welcome back to the channel'. Summarise it, then ask me what's missing before we write anything."

Prompt 2: outlier hunting (connect NexLev MCP first)

"Use NexLev MCP to find channels in [NICHE] under 6 months old with at least 3 videos above 100k views. For each, pull the 5 most recent and 5 best uploads. Flag channels where the best 5 are more than 5x the recent 5 (viral-spike traps, skip these). Return the survivors with estimated RPM, upload frequency and 48-hour view velocity on their last 3 uploads."

Prompt 3: packaging

"Here are 40 outlier titles from this niche. Reverse-engineer the psychological mechanism behind the clicks, not the surface pattern. Then write 25 titles for [TOPIC] built on those mechanisms, rank them by predicted CTR, and give me 3-5 words of thumbnail text for the top 5. Every thumbnail text needs an emotional verb."

Prompt 4: research brief (where Opus 5.5 earns its money)

"Research [TOPIC] and build a fact brief before any script gets written. Verify every date, name, location and quote against at least 2 sources. Flag anything where sources conflict. Mark anything you couldn't verify as UNVERIFIED instead of guessing. Then list the 5 most dramatic moments in chronological order with the source for each."

Prompt 5a: AI story script

"Using the fact brief and the channel bible, write a [LENGTH]-minute narration script. Cold open with a specific date, place and character in the first 15 seconds. 10 chapters. Cliffhangers at the end of chapters 3, 5, 7 and 9. Alternate high-tension scenes (3 minutes max) with slower character moments. The payoff lands at roughly 75% of runtime. The final chapter connects the story to something bigger. Follow every banned-phrase rule in the bible."

Prompt 5b: AI avatar script

"Rewrite the same story for an on-camera AI presenter. First person, direct to camera, sentences under 18 words so the lip sync stays natural. Mark every B-roll cutaway as [BROLL: description] and every emphasis beat as [PAUSE]. Keep the presenter on screen no more than 40 seconds at a time."

Prompt 6: visuals (connect Higgsfield MCP)

"Read the script and write one image prompt per scene change, around 18 total. Lock each character's age, face, clothing and hair across every prompt. Generate them through Higgsfield with GPT Images 2.0 in 16:9. Then pick the 3 most dramatic scenes and animate them with Seedance 2.5 at 8 seconds each for the intro and key beats."

Prompt 7: the edit list

"Turn the script and the generated assets into a timestamped edit decision list for CapCut. For every line: which asset is on screen, when to cut, where the slow zoom goes, where the animated clips sit, and which words the captions should emphasise. Output as a table I follow top to bottom."

Your editor (or you) stops making decisions and starts following instructions. A 1-hour video assembles in under 30 minutes.

You can also try using CapCut MCP for this, but it’s pretty ass ngl.

Prompt 8: the weekly audit

Export your YouTube Analytics as a CSV and drop it in:

"Find the 3 variables most correlated with videos beating my channel average. Look at publish day and time, title structure, thumbnail style, video length, topic, and the timestamp where retention dropped hardest. Then give me next week's 5 video ideas built on whatever's winning, with titles."

Run the text side of all 8 prompts through Claude and you're looking at roughly $1-2 of Opus 5.5 per finished video.

Opus 5.5 is cracked at reasoning, avoids stupid data mistakes, and sounds like a human for less than Fable 5.1, which you’ll notice immediately.

All PERFECT for avoiding shadowbans, demonetizations, and being attacked for spreading misinformation online - killing your channel trust - which would happen often if using cheaper models more prone to hallucination.

A few thoughts on agentic video editing I’ve had over the last few days:

1. 99% of ads should be edited agentically now. If your editors are still editing in the timeline, they’re falling behind. I got a message from my senior VE saying that he’s putting out 5x edits/day now at the same quality he was before.

2. The conversation with video editors will be uncomfortable because the timeline is all they’ve ever known. Some will be hesitant and some will be fearful for their job. I think the best way to address this is head on. The tech is inevitable, but having taste is still going to be incredibly valuable to train and give feedback to agents. Those who have this will become more valuable, those who don’t will struggle.

3. Opus 5.5 can natively edit all of your ads without needing any MCPs or plugins. I’ve tried the alternatives and couldn’t find anything that was significantly better than doing everything inside of Claude.

4. Have your senior editor(s) build skills for each style of edit (e.g. mashups, UGC, AI animations…). You can build these by feeding 4-5 inspo edits to Claude and tell it to make a skill out of it. I prefer building lots of mini-skills to one big video editing skill, so that the context stays as relevant as possible.

5. Once you have a base skill (e.g. ugly ads edits), the best way to train it is through feedback loops. Have the skill re-edit the last 25 ads each senior edited then put them in an artifact, and have the senior VE give feedback on each. Keep doing this until the skill is refined and it understands what a good edit is.

6. If you do this, there’s no reason why you shouldn’t be able to make edits that need little/no feedback. Most of ours are approved after v1 or v2, sometimes v3.

7. Only A-player editors should be training the skills.

8. Re adoption in the team, the AI champion builds the v1. Then get out of the way. I’m not the best editor on my team, so my job is to build the harness that lets the best editors train the skills, not build the skills myself.

9. If you want to supercharge this process, have your top editors record their screen as they edit. Turn on Gmeet or loom and get them to narrate the reasoning behind their process. E.g. why they chose this cut, pacing or b-roll clip…this is all context that gets fed into your skills.

10. It takes time to build, train and refine these skills. You have to go through the dip to get out the other side. Budget time in for senior VEs to work on this - otherwise you’ll end up with skills that put out subpar edits and don’t save you much/any time.

11. Operate under the assumption that this is the worst video editing is ever going to be. Opus 5.5 can do most of our editing today…what will Opus 6/Fable 6 be able to do? The editing skills you build are only going to become more valuable as the tech evolves.

I still don’t think people realise how big video editing being unblocked is. Things that I thought were 3-6 months away are now on the table.

Will continue to share more as I learn. CRAZY, crazy times.

My thumb rule for creating personal vibe coded software: if the existing one works and I have never felt any friction for 3 days in a row, then i’m good, let the experts handle it. If not, it’s worth a try.

The ones that have made it to the list

1. Video editor. I was on Davinci for some time, then I realised i don’t use 99.99% of the features, i only need ripple deleting a few parts. Then came across text based editing in Premiere pro, honestly life changing, the editing time came down significantly. For the past few weeks I realised the native transcript of premiere is horrible, and since I only do text based editing, that’s like the only thing I need. Tried importing the transcript from eleven labs but turns out it needs a converter which are mostly paid. 

So, after Fable dropped I gave it a try, took a few days of back and forth, since then all my YT videos are edited in there. I drop the video, it calls the eleven labs api, I edit and export, that’s it. Incredibly light weight, written in Swift, I wouldn’t say the rendering is faster than premiere pro but that was never a concern, I only do 1080p, so even for my hour long videos it takes 20 minutes. 

2. A pdf viewer and annotator written in swift. Adobe seemed too bloated.

3. An epub reader ios app. I come from android, recently switched to ios and I cannot stand any UI/UX apart from Lithium, but unfortunately that’s not in app store. So this one looks and feels exactly the same.

4. An app similar to Transmit to pull and push my files to Backblaze. 

We live in times.
